title: Confit de Canard
subtitle: French duck legs slow-cooked in their own fat
excerpt: Confit de canard is the great preserved meat of Gascony: duck legs cured in salt and then slow-cooked submerged in their own rendered fat until the meat is tender enough to fall from the bone. Finished in a hot pan until the skin is lacquer-crisp, it is one of the most deeply satisfying things to come from French cooking.
sourceNotes: Confit is an ancient French preservation technique in which meat is cured in salt and then cooked and stored in its own fat. Confit de canard is the most famous example, central to the cooking of Gascony and the Périgord in southwestern France. The fat-preserved duck will keep for weeks in the fridge. This recipe produces both the confit and usable flavoured duck fat for future cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in the fat. The confit keeps for up to 6 months frozen in fat.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch. The duck keeps for weeks in the fat in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 weeks ahead. Store in the fat in a sealed container in the fridge.

content.text: The salt cure does two things: it draws moisture from the meat, concentrating the flavour, and it seasons the meat all the way through. The cure takes a minimum of 4 hours, but overnight is better. Duck fat can be bought in tins or jars -- you need enough to submerge the legs. Lard is a reasonable substitute if duck fat is unavailable.

items.prepNote: or as much as needed to submerge the legs

content.text: Mix {{salt-flakes}} salt, crumbled {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves, {{thyme-fresh}} thyme, {{garlic}} garlic, and crushed {{black-peppercorns}} peppercorns together. Rub all over {{duck-leg}} duck legs. Arrange in a single layer in a dish. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight.

Preheat the oven to 140C. Rinse the cure from the duck legs and pat completely dry. Melt {{duck-fat}} duck fat in a deep ovenproof pan over low heat. Add the duck legs skin-side down. They should be fully submerged. Transfer to the oven and cook for 2 to 2.5 hours until the meat pulls easily from the bone.

Remove the legs from the fat. Either use immediately or store in the fat (pour fat over to cover completely and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks). To serve, place the legs skin-side down in a cold frying pan. Turn the heat to medium-high and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the skin is deeply golden and crisp. Serve with roast potatoes cooked in the rendered duck fat, and a green salad.

items.symptom: The skin is not crisp when finishing in the pan
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough, or the skin was still wet from the fat.
items.fix: Pat the skin dry before putting it in the pan. Start the duck in a cold pan and increase the heat slowly -- this renders the fat from the skin without burning the surface. The fat must render out before the skin can crisp. It takes 8 to 10 minutes.

content.text: Confit de canard is from Gascony and the Périgord, the duck-farming regions of southwestern France. The technique of preserving meat in fat dates back centuries and was the standard method for keeping duck and pork through the winter before refrigeration. Confit de canard is the defining ingredient of cassoulet from Castelnaudary. It is also eaten on its own with potatoes cooked in the duck fat -- this is one of the great simple meals of French country cooking.
